A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. Old assets are never overwritten and stay online afterward.

**Why the upload comes first:** The manifest switch is the moment users start receiving the new release. Once a browser loads the new manifest, it immediately requests the files the manifest names. If any of those files were still uploading, the request would return a 404 or a partial file, and the page would break or render without styles or scripts. Uploading everything first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens. The switch then flips the whole release at once instead of exposing a half-deployed state. If the upload fails partway, nothing user-facing has changed, and you can simply retry.

**Why the old assets are kept:** Browsers that loaded the page before the switch still hold the previous manifest. They keep requesting the old names as they lazy-load chunks, navigate within the app, or fetch images. CDN and browser caches may also serve the old manifest for a while after the switch. If the old files were deleted, those sessions would hit missing assets mid-use. Versioned names are what make keeping them possible: new files never overwrite old ones, so both releases can be served side by side. The same property makes rollback cheap. Pointing the manifest back at the previous names restores the prior release with no re-upload.

Each release happens in two steps, and the order matters.

1. **Upload every new asset under a versioned name.** Each file gets a name that changes whenever its content changes, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. Nothing references these files yet, so uploading them changes nothing users see.
2. **Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest tells browsers which asset files make up the current site. Changing it is the single step that releases the new version.

**Why the upload comes first:** once the manifest changes, any browser that loads it will immediately request the files it names. If any of those files are still uploading, the browser gets 404s and the page breaks or renders partly. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when the manifest goes live. Because the manifest switch is a single change, users get either the complete old version or the complete new one, never a mix.

**Why we keep the old assets:** a browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch still has those references. It will keep requesting the old files when it lazy-loads a route, fetches a chunk, or retries after a cache eviction. That can happen minutes or hours later in a long-lived tab. If we deleted the old files at release time, those users would hit 404s mid-session. Keeping the old files lets every session finish on the version it started with. It also makes rollback cheap: point the manifest back at the previous names, and nothing needs to be re-uploaded.

Versioned names make both steps safe. New files never overwrite old ones, so uploading can't disturb the live site, and a cache can never serve a stale file under a current name.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

If any of those files were still uploading, those browsers would get 404s and see a broken page. We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach browsers that already loaded the previous manifest. A page opened before the release keeps requesting the old asset names, for example when it lazy-loads a route or chunk later. If those files were deleted, that page would break partway through use. Because the names are versioned, old and new files can sit side by side without overwriting each other, so both releases stay complete.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names. The manifest is the only thing that changes what users get. Every file it references is immutable.

**Why the upload comes first.** As soon as the manifest switches, browsers start requesting whatever it names. If any of those files isn't uploaded yet, the page loads with a missing script or stylesheet and breaks. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when the first browser asks for it. The switch itself is a single small write, so the release goes live all at once and never half-deployed. Rolling back is the same move in reverse: point the manifest at the previous names.

**Why the old assets stay.** Switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that are already running. A page loaded a minute before the release still holds the old manifest and will keep requesting old asset names, for example when it lazy-loads a route chunk, fetches a font, or recovers from a dropped request. If those files were deleted, users who did nothing wrong would get 404s partway through a session. Keeping old assets lets every client finish on the version it started with. Because each name is unique to its content, old and new files never collide, and CDN and browser caches never serve a stale file under a current name.

**What this means for you.** Never upload a new file under an existing name, never switch the manifest before the upload has finished and been verified, and never delete old assets as part of a release.
